title: Climate debt

definition.text: The debt said to be owed by developed countries to developing ones for the damage caused by their far larger share of climate-changing emissions.

facts.text: It is part of the broader idea of ecological debt and was first put forward by NGOs in the 1990s.
Its two main parts are adaptation debt, help owed for adapting to climate change, and emissions debt, owed for excessive past emissions.
It gained attention at the 2009 Copenhagen conference, where developing countries led by Bolivia sought its repayment.
Support comes mainly from developing countries and environmental NGOs; criticism comes mostly from developed nations.
Critics argue that emissions made before their harm was understood, or by earlier generations, should not create guilt or debts.
Some say that, even if ethically sound, its adversarial framing may undermine climate negotiations.

contested_note: Developing countries and NGOs press for climate debt to be repaid, while developed nations and some analysts reject the idea that a debt is owed.

definition.text: The part of climate debt said to be owed by developed countries for having used more than their fair share of the atmosphere's capacity to absorb emissions.

facts.text: The atmosphere's capacity to absorb emissions is called the total carbon space; the claim is that rich countries overused their fair allocation of it.
Since around 1750 the United States alone has produced 25% of all carbon emissions, and developed countries together 70%.
Repayment would mean helping poorer countries industrialise cleanly and sharing out the remaining carbon space by population.

definition.text: The compensation developing countries claim they are owed for climate damage caused by the developed world's emissions.

facts.text: It rests on the idea that poorer nations suffer the worst consequences of a problem they did little to cause.
Lacking infrastructure and capital, poor countries often borrow at higher interest to recover from disasters, worsening their prospects.
The UNFCCC notes it can be met through financial aid and help coping with natural disasters.

title: Climate reparations

definition.text: Requested loss-and-damage payments for harm caused by climate change, framed as compensation owed for historical emissions and possibly including debt cancellation.

facts.text: Unlike plain 'loss and damage', the term treats compensation as an ethical and moral obligation that holds countries accountable for past emissions.
A 2023 study estimated that the top 21 fossil fuel companies will owe $5.4 trillion in cumulative reparations over 2025–2050.
Proposed channels include an international compensation commission, lawsuits, the polluter pays principle, debt forgiveness and direct grants.
The wealthiest nations have consistently opposed it at the UNFCCC, and before COP27 talks were steered to 'cooperation and facilitation' rather than liability.

contested_note: Developing nations and campaigners press for reparations, while rich nations oppose them and some argue current generations are not responsible for past emissions.

definition.text: A measurable long-term commitment in climate and energy policy, also called a climate goal or pledge, aimed at limiting climate change.

facts.text: Politicians set temperature targets based on research into the likely effects of different levels of warming, and these underpin carbon budgets and emission targets.
At least 164 countries have climate targets in their national legislation.
Under Kyoto, countries pledged an average 5.2 percent cut on 1990 levels over 2008 to 2012.
An emissions target may differ from a scientific carbon budget, since it can reflect political palatability rather than a specific temperature limit.
Many targets lie above the scientifically allowable emissions, and many rely on negative-emission technologies not yet developed.

title: Common But Differentiated Responsibilities

definition.text: The principle, set in the 1992 UN climate convention, that all countries share a duty to tackle environmental damage but not to the same degree.

facts.text: Because developed countries industrialised earlier and contributed more to climate change, they agreed to take greater responsibility for mitigation.
It can be seen as based on the polluter pays principle, with historical contribution and ability to act as the measures of responsibility.
Article 3 of the UNFCCC says developed countries should take the lead in combating climate change.
Under Kyoto it meant a rigid split in which only industrialised countries had strict limits; under Paris each country sets its own contribution as its circumstances change.
Critics argued it gave developing countries an unfair economic advantage; developing countries replied that their emissions are for survival while rich countries' are 'luxury emissions'.

prerequisites: United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change
related: Annex I and non-Annex I countries
contested_note: Some, including US negotiators, argue the rich–poor split is outdated or unfair, while developing countries defend it.
